title: Coaching, mentoring & emotional intelligence
blurb: Tell coaching from mentoring, explain why a coaching and mentoring style builds capability and engagement, and use Goleman's five components of emotional intelligence.
question: On an offshore wind cable project, the lead engineer snaps at colleagues in a review after a supplier delay. The project manager feels her own irritation rise. Later she wants to help him solve the resequencing problem himself rather than hand him an answer, and she also wants to help a junior planner think about his career. How do coaching, mentoring and emotional intelligence help her?

teach.body: COACHING helps a person improve their performance by finding their own solutions, mainly through skilful questioning and listening: the coachee owns the answer. MENTORING is a relationship in which an experienced person guides someone's longer-term development and career, sharing knowledge and advice. In plain English: a coach asks, a mentor shares. A coaching and mentoring style develops people, builds the team's capability and increases engagement.

rows.label: Project example
values: Helping a planner fix a clash

teach.h: Why a coaching and mentoring style matters
teach.body: It builds capability, so the PM can delegate more and the team copes without them. It increases engagement and ownership, because people grow and solve their own problems (Herzberg's motivators of responsibility and growth). It improves resilience and succession, and helps retain good people. The trade-off: it takes time, and it doesn't suit a crisis or someone with no grounding in the task, who needs direction first. In iterative teams, coaching helps the team learn to self-organise.

steps.label: Reality
steps.sub: 'What's happening now? What have you tried?'

steps.label: Way forward
steps.sub: 'What will you do, and by when?'

teach.caption: One widely used structure is GROW (Goal, Reality, Options, Will or Way forward). The coach asks; the coachee decides.

teach.body: Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise and manage your own emotions, and to recognise and influence the emotions of others. Goleman describes five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. It underpins trust, conflict handling and influencing, which are exactly what a PM needs when leading people they may have no authority over, through pressure, change and disagreement.

teach.body: After a supplier delay, lead engineer Tom snaps in a review. Grace notices her own irritation (self-awareness) and stays calm (self-regulation). Afterwards she talks to him privately and realises he fears for his reputation (empathy). She coaches: 'What would a good outcome look like? What options do we have?' Tom proposes a resequencing plan, and Grace wins the sponsor's support for it (social skills). Separately, she mentors a junior planner monthly on his career.

teach.text: Common confusions. Coaching is NOT telling people the answer: it uses questions so they find their own. Mentoring DOES draw on the mentor's experience and advice. EI is not just 'being nice' or avoiding conflict: it is using emotional awareness to handle conflict well. And Goleman's five include MOTIVATION, not 'self-actualisation' (Maslow).

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define coaching (questions, own solutions, performance) and mentoring (experienced guide, career and development).
Explain the importance: builds capability, engagement and ownership; frees the PM to delegate; aids retention and succession.
Name Goleman's five EI components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
Link EI to the PM's job: trust, handling conflict, influencing stakeholders without authority, staying calm under pressure.
Apply to the scenario, and note limits: in a crisis or with a complete novice, direct first, coach later.
Coaching: questioning and listening so people find their own solutions; focus on performance.
Mentoring: an experienced person guides someone's longer-term career and development.
A coaching and mentoring style builds capability, engagement and ownership.
Goleman's EI: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
EI underpins trust, conflict handling and influencing.

summary: You can now tell coaching from mentoring and explain why a coaching and mentoring style matters for a project team. You can also name Goleman's five components of emotional intelligence and show how each helps a project manager build trust, handle conflict and influence others.

A.q: Which BEST describes coaching in a project leadership context?
options: Telling someone the right answer from experience
Helping someone find their own answers by asking
Directing someone step by step through the task
Assessing someone's performance for an appraisal
A.why: Coaching uses questions and listening to help people find their own solutions and improve their performance.

whyNot.0: Sharing answers from experience is closer to mentoring or instructing.
whyNot.2: Step-by-step direction is a directing style, not coaching.
whyNot.3: Appraisal judges performance; coaching helps improve it.

A.q: Which is NOT one of Goleman's five components of emotional intelligence?
options: Self-awareness
Empathy
Self-regulation
Self-actualisation
A.why: Self-actualisation is the top of Maslow's hierarchy. Goleman's five are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

whyNot.0: Self-awareness is one of Goleman's five.
whyNot.1: Empathy is one of Goleman's five.
whyNot.2: Self-regulation is one of Goleman's five.

A.q: A senior project manager meets a junior colleague monthly to share experience and advise on career choices. This is BEST described as:
options: Mentoring
Coaching
Delegating
Directing
A.why: An experienced person guiding someone's longer-term development and career is mentoring.

whyNot.1: Coaching relies on questions so the person finds their own answers, usually on specific performance goals.
whyNot.2: Delegating hands over a task; it isn't about career guidance.
whyNot.3: Directing gives instructions on a task.

B.q: Why is a coaching style valuable for a project manager?
options: It removes the need to set clear objectives
It is the fastest way to handle a live crisis
It builds capability so more can be delegated
It means the PM no longer has to give feedback
B.why: Coaching develops people's ability to solve problems themselves, which builds capability and lets the PM delegate more.

whyNot.0: Coaching still needs clear goals; the first coaching question is often about the goal.
whyNot.1: In a crisis, direction is usually faster; coaching takes time.
whyNot.3: Feedback remains part of developing people.

B.q: A project manager notices she becomes short-tempered when sponsors change priorities late, and now pauses before responding. Which EI components is she showing?
options: Self-awareness and self-regulation
Empathy and social skills
Motivation and empathy
Social skills and motivation
B.why: Noticing her own reaction is self-awareness; pausing to control it is self-regulation.

whyNot.1: Empathy and social skills concern other people's emotions and relationships, not managing her own reaction.
whyNot.2: Motivation is inner drive towards goals; empathy is reading others. Neither fits.
whyNot.3: Neither component describes noticing and controlling her own temper.

B.q: In which situation is a coaching style LEAST appropriate?
options: A capable analyst wants to improve her reports
A brand-new starter lacks basic task knowledge
A team lead is weighing options for a problem
An engineer wants to improve his presenting
B.why: Coaching relies on the person having enough knowledge to find their own answers. A complete novice needs direction and instruction first.

whyNot.0: A capable person improving a skill is ideal for coaching.
whyNot.2: Helping someone weigh options is a classic coaching conversation.
whyNot.3: Improving an existing skill suits coaching well.

C.q: During a tense review, a stakeholder angrily blames the project team for delays. Which response shows the HIGHEST emotional intelligence from the project manager?
options: Defend the team firmly and point out his errors
Say nothing now and avoid him for a few weeks
Agree with him to end the conversation quickly
Stay calm, acknowledge his concern, then explore
C.why: Staying calm (self-regulation), acknowledging his feelings (empathy) and then exploring the issue together (social skills) shows high EI.

whyNot.0: A defensive counter-attack escalates the conflict and shows little self-regulation.
whyNot.1: Avoiding him leaves the issue unresolved and damages the relationship.
whyNot.2: Agreeing just to end the conversation sacrifices the team and the truth.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about coaching and mentoring are correct?
1. Coaching focuses on improving performance through questioning
2. A mentor must be the mentee's line manager
3. Mentoring draws on the mentor's experience to guide development
4. Coaching requires the coach to be the subject expert
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Coaching uses questioning to improve performance (1); mentoring uses the mentor's experience to guide development (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: mentors are often outside the line, which helps openness.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: mentors needn't be line managers, and coaches needn't be subject experts.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: coaching relies on coaching skill, not subject expertise.

C.q: An iterative team keeps asking its project manager to decide how to split user stories. The PM wants the team to self-organise. Which response BEST reflects a coaching style?
options: 'What options do you see, and which would you pick?'
'Split them by screen; I'll check them all tonight.'
'Ask the product owner; it's not my decision now.'
'Use the split from last sprint; it worked fine then.'
C.why: Open questions hand the thinking back to the team, building the capability it needs to self-organise.

whyNot.1: This directs and checks, keeping the team dependent on the PM.
whyNot.2: Redirecting avoids the question without developing the team's ability.
whyNot.3: Giving a ready-made answer is telling, not coaching.

reteach.title: Think of a young band
reteach.question: A young band wants to get better and get noticed. A music teacher, a veteran musician and their band leader all help in different ways. Who is coaching, who is mentoring, and where does emotional intelligence come in?

blocks.body: The music teacher asks the guitarist: 'What did you hear in that solo? What could you try instead?' That is coaching: questions that help her find her own improvement. A veteran musician meets the band now and then and shares stories and advice about touring and record deals: mentoring. The band leader notices the drummer is upset after a bad gig, keeps her own frustration in check and talks it through: emotional intelligence.

blocks.text: A coach asks, a mentor shares. Both develop people; EI is what makes either relationship work.

explain.body: Coaching helps someone improve performance on specific goals by asking open questions and listening, so they find their own solutions. The coach needs coaching skill more than subject expertise. It builds capability and ownership.

test.q: Which question is MOST typical of a coach?
options: 'Why didn't you follow the plan?'
'Here's how I would fix it.'
'What could you try next?'
'Have you finished it yet?'
test.why: An open, forward-looking question invites the person to find their own solution: the essence of coaching.

whyNot.0: This is a blaming question that tends to make people defensive.
whyNot.1: This gives the answer rather than drawing it out.
whyNot.3: This is a closed status check, not a development question.

explain.body: Mentoring is a longer-term relationship in which an experienced person guides someone's development and career, sharing knowledge, perspective and advice. The mentor is often outside the mentee's line, which encourages open conversations.

items.label: the mentor shares what they know

test.q: What MOST distinguishes mentoring from coaching?
options: Mentoring avoids giving any advice at all
Mentoring draws on the mentor's experience
Mentoring only happens in a crisis situation
Mentoring is a short, task-focused session
test.why: A mentor shares their own experience and advice to guide someone's longer-term development.

whyNot.0: Mentors do give advice; it's coaches who mainly ask rather than tell.
whyNot.2: Mentoring is an ongoing relationship, not a crisis tool.
whyNot.3: Short, task-focused sessions describe coaching more than mentoring.

explain.body: Self-awareness: knowing your emotions. Self-regulation: managing your reactions. Motivation: inner drive towards goals. Empathy: sensing others' feelings. Social skills: building rapport, influencing and handling conflict.

explain.caption: The first three are about managing yourself; the last two are about managing relationships.

test.q: A PM senses that a usually chatty team member has gone quiet and seems anxious, and checks in with her privately. Which EI component is the PM MAINLY using?
options: Self-regulation
Motivation
Self-awareness
Empathy
test.why: Recognising and responding to another person's feelings is empathy.

whyNot.0: Self-regulation is about managing your own reactions.
whyNot.1: Motivation is your own inner drive towards goals.
whyNot.2: Self-awareness is recognising your own emotions, not someone else's.

explain.body: Project managers lead through influence, often without authority, under pressure and change. EI underpins the trust that makes people speak up, the calm needed to handle conflict well and the empathy and social skill to influence stakeholders and the team.

test.q: Why is emotional intelligence especially important for project managers?
options: It underpins trust, influence and handling conflict
It replaces the need for planning and control
It guarantees the team will never disagree
It is a formal requirement at each decision gate
test.why: PMs rely on trust and influence and must handle conflict under pressure; EI underpins all three.

whyNot.1: EI complements planning and control; it doesn't replace them.
whyNot.2: Disagreement still happens; EI helps handle it constructively.
whyNot.3: Decision gates assess the business case and plans, not the PM's EI.
